extracted.intended_audience: practitioners in PTAB IPR proceedings (patent attorneys, litigators, expert witnesses)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for using expert witness testimony in PTAB inter partes review (IPR) proceedings, including admissibility, qualifications, reliance on prior declarations, depositions, substitution, and how the Board weighs expert evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Rule of Evidence 702 requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert who is qualified by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education may testify in the form of an opinion or otherwise only if: (a) the expert’s specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact; (b) the testimony is based on sufficient facts or data; (c) the testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods; and (d) the expert has reliably applied those principles and methods to the facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four-prong FRE 702 test governs admissibility of expert testimony in PTAB proceedings where FRE apply (see 37 C.F.R. § 42.62). Practitioners should address each prong in declarations and anticipate challenges directed to sufficiency of facts/data, reliability of methods, and proper application to the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert declaration as direct testimony / evidentiary role
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert declaration submitted to the Board is a form of direct testimony/evidence and can substitute for taking direct witness testimony at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because declarations serve as direct evidence, they are subject to being tested by cross-examination and other forms of challenge. Declarations should therefore include underlying facts and data supporting opinions. Treat declarations with the same preparation and evidentiary rigor as live testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinions must be supported by underlying facts and data; patent-law opinions not admissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert opinions must be supported by sufficient facts and data and must be the product of reliable principles and methods; testimony on U.S. patent law itself is not admissible from experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations should tie opinions explicitly to factual bases and technical data. Parties should avoid submitting expert opinions that purport to interpret or state conclusions of law about claim construction or patentability; legal conclusions are for the Board, not the expert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification / ordinary skill in the art requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To offer expert testimony from the perspective of a skilled artisan, a witness must at least have ordinary skill in the art relevant to the patent at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board will evaluate qualifications; Best Medical (Fed. Cir. 2022) provides a non-exhaustive list of factors that may guide the factfinder in assessing level of skill in the art: (1) inventor's educational level; (2) types of problems encountered in the art; (3) prior art solutions; (4) rapidity of innovations; (5) sophistication of the technology; (6) educational level of active workers in the field. Use these factors when describing an expert's background and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance / scope of expert’s experience must be commensurate with testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert’s qualifications must be commensurate with the scope of the testimony offered; experience in a different field may be challenged as not qualifying the witness for the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an expert's background is in a different but arguably related field, parties should submit supplemental information establishing relevance (and be prepared for the Board to allow discovery so the opponent can challenge it). Consider tailoring testimony to the expert's demonstrable areas of competence and clearly explain how experience transfers to the claimed technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior declarations / testimony from other proceedings (hearsay issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations or transcripts from other proceedings may raise hearsay issues when used in a new IPR; they are prior testimony and may be admissible only under exceptions (e.g., FRE 804(b)(1) if declarant is unavailable and the party had an opportunity and similar motive to develop the testimony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on prior declarations or transcripts, address hearsay concerns and whether an exception applies. Expect patent owner to move to compel the declarant for deposition or to strike the declaration if cross-examination is not available. The Board may weigh such evidence less if cross-examination cannot be compelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge to copied declarations (copied from another IPR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting a declaration copied from another IPR can prompt motions to compel the expert for deposition or motions to strike the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reusing prior declarations, be prepared for the opponent to seek cross-examination or to argue inadmissibility. The Board may authorize a subpoena for deposition, strike the declaration, or caution that the declaration may be inadmissible without cross-examination. Avoid wholesale copying without addressing context/reliability and availability for cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and deposition rules applicable in IPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB procedural rules govern discovery and taking of testimony in IPRs: 37 C.F.R. § 42.51 (discovery, including cross-examination of affidavit testimony), § 42.53 (taking testimony; manner of taking deposition testimony; transcript handling and exhibit filing), § 42.62 (FRE apply), § 42.63 (forms of evidence), § 42.64 (objections, motions to exclude), § 42.65 (expert testimony; tests and data), and content rules for petitions/responses (e.g., § 42.105(a)(5), § 42.107).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must follow the cited regulations: e.g., cross-examination of affidavit testimony is authorized within Board-set time periods (42.51); the proponent of testimony must generally provide transcript copies to parties and file testimony as an exhibit (42.53(f)(7)). Use these provisions to plan timing for depositions, exhibits, and motions to exclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions of experts are not routine discovery depositions (limitations and forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions of experts in PTAB proceedings are not ordinary discovery depositions; their taking and use are governed by PTAB rules and the Board’s scheduling/authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While expert depositions are subject to Board control and not free-form discovery, cross-examination of affidavit testimony is authorized as routine discovery under § 42.51(b)(1)(ii) within set periods. Parties should move timely to compel depositions or cross-examination when needed and be mindful of Board orders that may limit routine discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight to give absence of patent owner expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: If a petitioner presents an expert declaration and the patent owner does not present expert testimony in opposition, the Board should weigh the evidence but not shift the burden to the patent owner to present expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Fanduel v. Interactive Games (Fed. Cir. 2020), IPR regulations do not require a patent owner to submit a response; the burden remains on petitioner. The Board may consider the patent owner's lack of expert testimony as a factor, but cannot treat lack of rebuttal as automatic judgment for petitioner without weighing the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on cross-examination of a party’s own expert (using opponent’s examination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the opponent’s cross-examination of a party’s own expert (e.g., relying on that cross-examination in reply) raises issues about whether the proponent can rely on such testimony and whether it is fair or admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 42.53 requires transcript handling and exhibit filing. The Board may treat the cross-examination as part of the record, but opponents may move to strike testimony or preclude reliance if fairness or reliability concerns exist. Be prepared to defend reliance on such cross-examination and for motions to exclude if misuse is alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of experts after withdrawal
rubrics_metrics.description: If an expert withdraws after institution and a party seeks to substitute a new expert who adopts the withdrawing expert’s testimony, the Board will consider prejudice to the opponent and whether the substitute is available for cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board has allowed substitution in at least one case (Alzehon v. Risen IPR2021-00347) but may condition substitution on availability for cross-examination or deny substitution as prejudicial. The Board may also authorize subpoenas to obtain information about withdrawal. Parties seeking substitution should propose conditions (e.g., availability to be deposed) to mitigate prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony cannot substitute for disclosure in a prior art reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony cannot supply missing disclosure in a cited reference; experts cannot be used to fill gaps in what a reference actually discloses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the Consolidated Trial Practice Guide: experts should not be used to supply factual disclosures that are absent from the prior art. When arguing obviousness or anticipation, make record-based showings of what references disclose rather than relying on expert extrapolation to create missing elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness considerations: cross-examination, hearsay, and weighing of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Board must consider fairness issues about cross-examination availability, hearsay status of prior testimony, whether a party can compel cross-examination, and whether hearsay exceptions apply; these considerations affect admissibility, weight, or exclusion of expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning use of expert evidence, anticipate and address: (1) whether prior testimony is hearsay and whether an exception (e.g., FRE 804(b)(1)) applies; (2) whether cross-examination can be compelled or ordered; (3) whether absence of cross-examination suggests lowering the weight of the evidence or exclusion on fairness grounds. Be proactive in proposing discovery and in justifying the evidentiary approach to the Board.
